meta.titre: What Makes Islam Distinct: tawhid, the final revelation and the Muslim attitude to other faiths
meta.sous_theme: Distinctive beliefs of Islam, relations with other religions and Surah 109
tags: A Level Religious Studies - islam and other faiths

source.epreuve_titre: GCE A/L Religious Studies past paper (Cameroon)

sections.contenu_markdown: In many Cameroonian towns a mosque, a church and a traditional shrine can be found within a short walk of one another. Neighbours of different faiths trade in the same market and celebrate each other's festivals. Examiners therefore ask two linked questions: what is particular about Islam when it is placed beside other religions, and what attitude does Islam teach towards people who follow another faith or reject faith altogether.

items: Islam means submission to the will of Allah, and a Muslim is one who submits.
Muslims believe that the Quran was revealed to the Prophet Muhammad through the angel Jibril (Gabriel).
Judaism, Christianity and Islam are called Abrahamic faiths because each traces its faith back to Abraham (Ibrahim in Islam).

sections.titre: Distinctive features of Islam and the Muslim attitude to people of other faiths
sections.contenu_markdown:
### Features Muslims regard as particular to Islam
| Feature | What Muslims believe |
|---|---|
| Tawhid, the oneness of God | Allah is one, without partner, equal or offspring. The gravest sin is shirk, associating anything with God. Surah 112 (Al-Ikhlas) is a short statement of this belief. |
| The Quran as final revelation | Muslims hold that the Quran is the word of God itself, given in Arabic through Jibril to Muhammad and preserved in its original wording. |
| Muhammad, the seal of the prophets | Muhammad is the last of the messengers, so no new prophet or new scripture is expected. |
| Respect for earlier prophets | Muslims honour Adam, Ibrahim, Musa, Dawud and Isa (Jesus) among others. They hold that Isa was a prophet born of the virgin Maryam, but not divine. The Quran has a Surah named after Maryam. |
| Earlier scriptures | The Torah, the Psalms and the Gospel are respected as revealed to earlier prophets, but Muslims hold that the Quran completes and corrects the message because earlier texts were altered over time. |
| A complete way of life | The Shariah guides worship, family life, business and morals, so religion is not limited to the mosque. |
| No priesthood | There is no ordained clergy mediating between worshippers and God. An imam leads prayer but has no sacramental power. |

### Attitude to other faiths
- **No compulsion in religion**: the Quran teaches that faith cannot be forced (Surah 2, verse 256).
- **People of the Book (Ahl al-Kitab)**: Jews and Christians are given special respect because they received scriptures, and in Muslim societies they were traditionally protected communities.
- **Firmness in worship**: Muslims worship Allah alone and do not join in the worship of others.

### Surah 109 (Al-Kafirun)
This short Makkan Surah has six verses. The Prophet is told to declare that he does not worship what the unbelievers worship and that they do not worship what he worships. The last verse is understood to mean 'for you your religion, for me mine'. Scholars read it in two ways: as a refusal to mix worship or compromise on tawhid, and as a statement that each person is free in religious choice. A good answer presents both readings.

variantes.nom: Question asking what is particular of Islam among religions
variantes.quand_utiliser: When asked to show distinctiveness or compare Islam with other faiths.
variantes.contenu_markdown: Select four or five features (tawhid, final revelation, seal of the prophets, view of Isa, no priesthood). For each, begin with 'Muslims believe' or 'Muslims hold', explain it, and then state in respectful words how it differs from other faiths. Never ridicule another religion.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When a Surah such as 109 is cited and you must discuss its message.
variantes.contenu_markdown: Name the Surah, give its setting and length, state its message, explain how Muslims apply it to relations with others, give more than one interpretation, and conclude with a judgement.

sections.enonce_markdown: Examine how the Muslim belief in the oneness of God shapes the way Islam is distinct from other faiths. (25 marks)

etapes.action: Analyse the command word and the key idea.
etapes.justification: 'Examine' asks for close explanation. The key idea is tawhid and its consequences.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Start from tawhid, then trace what follows from it.

etapes.justification: A precise definition earns the first marks.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Tawhid is the belief that Allah is one and without partner, equal or offspring; shirk is associating anything with Him.

etapes.justification: Linking the principle to teachings shows understanding.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Muslims therefore honour Isa as a prophet and not as divine; they hold that the Quran, as the word of God, is final; and they believe no priest stands between a person and God.

etapes.action: Show the consequences for practice and attitude.
etapes.justification: Practice proves that the belief is lived.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Worship is directed to Allah alone in the daily prayers facing Makkah; images of God are not used; Muslims keep to their own worship yet respect Jews and Christians as People of the Book, as the Quran teaches that faith may not be forced.

etapes.justification: A final judgement completes an 'examine' answer.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Tawhid is the centre of the differences, although Islam also shares much with Judaism and Christianity, such as belief in one God and respect for Ibrahim and Musa.

sections.conclusion_markdown: Model answer, in brief. Tawhid, the oneness of Allah, is the centre of Islamic belief. From it follow the Muslim view of Isa as a prophet and not as divine, the status of the Quran as the final and preserved word of God, the absence of a priesthood and the direction of all worship to Allah alone. Islam also has features in common with other faiths, such as belief in one God and honour for earlier prophets, so its distinctiveness lies in how these shared ideas are understood. Towards followers of other faiths the Quran teaches that faith may not be forced, and Muslims show particular respect for the People of the Book.

items.pourquoi_faux: Muslims worship Allah alone. Muhammad is honoured as the last messenger but is not worshipped.
items.correction_markdown: 'Muslims worship Allah only and honour Muhammad as the final prophet.'

items.erreur_markdown: 'Muslims do not believe in Jesus or Moses.'
items.pourquoi_faux: Muslims honour Isa and Musa as prophets and believe in the virgin birth of Isa. What differs is the Muslim understanding of Isa's identity.
items.correction_markdown: 'Muslims honour Isa as a prophet born of Maryam, but they do not hold that he is divine.'

items.erreur_markdown: Using insulting or biased language about another religion.
items.pourquoi_faux: Religious Studies answers must be neutral and respectful; bias shows poor method and may cost marks.
items.correction_markdown: Describe differences with phrases such as 'Christians believe ...' and 'Muslims hold ...'.

items.erreur_markdown: Mixing up the Quran and the hadith.
items.pourquoi_faux: The Quran is regarded as the word of God, while the hadith are reports of the sayings and actions of the Prophet.
items.correction_markdown: Name the source accurately and say which is Quran and which is hadith.

items.erreur_markdown: Listing features of Islam without saying how they make Islam distinct.
items.pourquoi_faux: The question asks what is particular. A list shows knowledge but not understanding of difference.
items.correction_markdown: After each feature add a sentence beginning 'This distinguishes Islam because ...'.

items.enonce_markdown: State four beliefs or practices of Islam that Muslims regard as particular to their faith.
items.solution_markdown: Any four of: (1) tawhid, the oneness of Allah; (2) the Quran as the final revelation in Arabic; (3) Muhammad as the seal of the prophets; (4) no priesthood standing between worshipper and God; (5) the Shariah as a complete way of life; (6) respect for Isa as a prophet but not as divine. **Four clear points earn full marks.**

items.enonce_markdown: Explain how Islam views Isa (Jesus) and why this view marks a difference from Christian belief.
items.solution_markdown: Model points. Muslims honour Isa as a great prophet, born of the virgin Maryam, who worked miracles by God's permission. They reject the idea that he is the Son of God or part of a Trinity, because they hold that Allah is one and has no offspring or partner. Christians believe that Jesus is the Son of God and the Saviour, so the two faiths differ on his identity, although both honour him. **A mark for each accurate belief, with both traditions described neutrally.**

items.enonce_markdown: 'The Muslim attitude towards those of other faiths combines firmness in belief with respect for people.' Discuss with reference to the Quran.
items.solution_markdown: Plan. Firmness: tawhid forbids joining other worship, and Surah 109 declares separation in worship. Respect: faith may not be forced; Jews and Christians are People of the Book who received scriptures; the last verse of Surah 109 is read by many as accepting freedom of religion. Counter-view: some interpretations stress separation more than coexistence, and history shows both cooperation and conflict. **Conclusion: the statement is largely accurate if firmness is understood as concerning worship and respect as concerning persons.**

items_markdown: Tawhid, the oneness of Allah, is the centre of the features that make Islam distinct; shirk is its opposite and the gravest sin.
Muslims regard the Quran as God's own word, preserved in Arabic, and Muhammad as the seal of the prophets.
Islam honours earlier prophets, including Isa, but does not hold that Isa is divine.
The Quran teaches that there is no compulsion in religion, and Jews and Christians are respected as People of the Book.
Surah 109 can be read as firmness in worship and as freedom of religious choice; a good answer presents both.
